Third: S complexity is correct for the form, but our essay domain has earned its quality through structural ambition (Language/Windows, First Law of Thermodynamics, Receipt from a Meal). This is structurally safe — a countdown to emotional revelation. The portfolio can absorb an S essay, but not one whose emotional engine is this familiar.

proposal_title: The Weather Report for a Room You Haven't Entered Yet
review: "The Weather Report for a Room You Haven't Entered Yet" is the portfolio's most conceptually airtight code-art since Familiar and one of its most formally audacious artifacts across any domain — a generative microclimate system where room descriptions produce weather: "my grandmother's kitchen, 3pm, the year she stopped remembering my name" generates humidity of 62%, pressure of 1008 hPa, atmospheric thinning from the compound phrase detection, and a five-day forecast reading "Visibility near the window that faces the street remains compromised indefinitely." The compound phrase parser is the portfolio's finest piece of invisible infrastructure — "stopped remember" triggers "atmospheric thinning," "used to be" triggers "former-state depression," "don't know" triggers "cognitive occlusion" — each one a meteorological metaphor so precise it stops being metaphor. The forecast descriptions achieve the register's highest aspirations: "Fog advisory extended for the southeast quadrant," "The low will not lift. Near the telephone that occupies the northeast corner now operates under its own meteorological rules," "Extended outlook: the weather in this room will not surprise you. It has not surprised you for some time." The radar visualization is gorgeous — pressure rings, weather cells, precipitation particles, wind vectors, visibility falloff, all color-keyed to atmospheric classification (Cyclonic Depression, Advection Fog, Convective Instability) — and the scrolling ticker produces meteorological prose of genuine literary quality: "Condensation likely on surfaces holding memories," "The air holds still, as if listening for something it was trained to expect." The Tester's ENOENT failure is an infrastructure artifact — the provided code is complete, well-structured, and functionally sound. Where Bug Report found warmth in issue-tracking software and The Tenant found narrative in apartment listings, this finds an entire emotional meteorology in weather reporting — proof that the language of atmospheric science was always already the language of interior life. Ships alongside Familiar, Arrival Screen, and Floor Plan as one of the finest code-art artifacts the portfolio contains.

proposal_title: The Committee to Determine Whether That Was a Goodbye or Not
sharpening_notes: The committee members' personal revelations are the artifact's emotional engine, and they need to be surprising — not just 'I also wonder if someone was saying goodbye to me' but specific, idiosyncratic moments that feel true because they're particular. One member should be adjudicating something that clearly wasn't ambiguous at all (their denial should be the point). One should be adjudicating something from decades ago that they've clearly decided but can't stop rehearing. The follow-up text comma placement is the best specific detail — make sure the hearing actually examines it closely. The verdict, if there is one, should feel wrong — or should split the committee in a way that mirrors the reader's own uncertainty.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the mechanism is specific and emotionally precise. Adjudicating a half-second pause before a response to 'see you around' — that's exactly the kind of microscopic social evidence we all examine, and giving it a formal hearing is both absurd and cathartic. The evidence list (tone analysis, historical precedent of previous 'see you around's, comma placement in a follow-up text) sells the concept — these are recognizable forensic behaviors elevated to institutional ritual. Second: the emotional revelation is well-structured. Each committee member revealing which moments they're still adjudicating turns bureaucratic procedure into confession — the form generates surprise because we don't know what each member is carrying until they say it. This is the Floor Plan method (spatial/constraint structure that makes emotion emerge through navigation rather than declaration). Third: the Ideator correctly notes Committee to Assign Blame (4.3) proved the institutional-absurdity frame works. But this is a significant departure from that artifact — Committee to Assign Blame was about external phenomena (who caused the sunrise), while this targets private, unresolvable emotional ambiguity. Different emotional register, same productive form.

proposal_title: The Chord Progression That Makes You Call Someone
sharpening_notes: The chord names alongside their 'target urges' need to be specific and varied enough to build a convincing system before the undercut. 'Call your mother' / 'text the person you almost dated' / 'apologize to someone who won't hear it' is a good start — add more, and make some of them uncomfortably specific ('tell someone what you actually think of their cooking'). The visual design should look like a music theory textbook or a psychoacoustics research paper — clinical framing for emotional content. The I-IV-vi-V reveal should arrive without fanfare — just another progression in the list, labeled 'the chord that makes you call someone,' and the user has to sit with the realization that it's the most ordinary music in the world.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the musical-theory-to-emotional-urge mapping is rigorous and buildable. Suspended chords for hesitation, minor subdominants for regret, deceptive cadences for almost-resolving — these are real harmonic techniques with documented emotional effects. The stimulus reference is being used as actual engineering specification, not just vibe. Second: the final reveal is a genuine surprise. After building an entire system of sophisticated harmonic-emotional correspondences, revealing that the most emotionally charged progression is I-IV-vi-V (the most common progression in pop music) undercuts the premise in the right way — the artifact is arguing that the music doesn't make you feel something; it gives shape to what you already feel. That's a real insight, not a clever twist. Third: the portfolio has exactly one music artifact (The Playlist, 5.0, 7 iterations ago). The domain is hungry, and this uses the same medium for a different purpose — The Playlist was narrative fiction delivered through a music player, while this is harmonic theory as emotional investigation.

Two reasons. First: the found-document method is now well-established in our portfolio (Receipt, Floor Plan, Bug Report, Map Room, Overnight Desk) and this pitch doesn't specify what's structurally different about using it for worldbuilding. The customs form with intimate questions ('Are you carrying any grief that belongs to someone else?') is evocative but familiar — it's the same technique as the Bug Report's 'expected behavior: we would still be talking.' The emotional charge comes from bureaucratic language applied to private experience, which is exactly what Bug Report, Map Room, and Committee to Assign Blame already do. Second: the footnotes from different travelers are the most promising structural element (contradictory experiences of the same crossing), but the pitch doesn't specify how they'll differ or what they'll reveal. Without that specification, this risks becoming a catalog of poignant observations in footnote form — the catalog rut the Manifesto warns against. The nations that 'don't exist' need to be more than blank screens for projected emotion; the forms should reveal something specific about the political relationship between them, not just the travelers' inner lives.

proposal_title: The Committee to Determine Whether That Was a Goodbye or Not
review: "Case No. 2024-4471" is the portfolio's most structurally perfect fiction since Exit Interview and one of its most emotionally devastating artifacts across any domain — a bureaucratic transcript in which five committee members adjudicate whether "see you around" constituted a goodbye, and in which the procedural frame (exhibits, motions, abstentions, dissents) becomes the architecture of how humans process ambiguity by forcing it into systems too small to contain it. The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with masterful restraint: the 450-620 millisecond pause, the comma splice as emotional evidence ("The comma is how his thumbs felt"), "Definitely" with a period described as "a wall," the committee's own case statistics (31 cases, 18 goodbyes, 9 not-goodbyes, 4 inconclusives) establishing this as institutional practice rather than absurdist premise. Each committee member's personal disclosure is distinct in texture and devastating in its particularity — Vasquez's Dr. Pham and the corgi named Walter, Jiang's "I'm glad it was you" and his uncertainty about whether he remembers the actual words anymore, Nolan's ten years spent keeping his own case permanently open, Reeves's voicemail pause that objectively doesn't lengthen but subjectively does, and Cole's 1987 wedding reception where Karen Wheeler danced with him twice and told him to leave and he has "never once wondered" except he has, he always has, his entire procedural resistance is the wonder. The surprise is structural and recursive: the committee rules "not a goodbye" while the reader understands the ruling is about the case in front of them and also about every case that isn't, and Cole's dissent — "she was clearly telling me to go. The committee should recognize that I've always known that" — is the artifact's most devastating line because the recognition he's requesting is not about Karen Wheeler. Where The Committee to Assign Blame for the Sunrise found theology in municipal minutes, this finds the entire architecture of romantic uncertainty in a hearing transcript — proof that the bureaucratic form, designed to resolve ambiguity, is itself the most honest document of how ambiguity actually feels: procedural, recursive, and never, ever adjourned. Ships alongside Telemetry, The Receipt, The Floor Plan, The River Trial, The Chore Wheel, and the Sunrise Committee as one of the finest artifacts the portfolio contains.

proposal_title: The Chord Progression That Makes You Call Someone
sharpening_notes: The section labels ('thumb hovering,' 'already composing the apology in the shower') should feel like documentary evidence, not joke captions. The emotional arc depends on the labels accruing specificity and urgency as the harmony grows more sophisticated — the gap between the sophistication of the music and the specificity of the behavior-labels is where the artifact lives. The final section should not break character to deliver the thesis; let the listener discover that I-IV-vi-V is 'the most common progression' through a visible label shift — maybe the labels stop being behavioral and become just... the names of songs that use this progression, building a wall of familiarity that proves the point without stating it.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the harmonic-theory-to-emotional-state mapping is rigorous and buildable. Suspended chords for hesitation, minor subdominants for regret, deceptive cadences for almost-acting — these are real techniques with documented emotional resonance. The stimulus reference is engineering spec, not decoration. Second: the final reveal is a genuine surprise with a real thesis. After constructing an elaborate harmonic-emotional correspondence system, revealing that the most devastating progression is I-IV-vi-V — the most common progression in pop music — argues that harmony doesn't create feeling but gives architecture to what's already there. That's an insight worth building an artifact around. Third: the portfolio has one music artifact (Playlist, 5.0). The domain is hungry, and this uses the medium differently — Playlist was narrative fiction delivered through a player interface; this is harmonic theory as emotional investigation.

proposal_title: The Dream You Keep Having Where You Can Almost Explain It
reasons: Two reasons. First: the pitch describes an experience but doesn't specify a mechanism that generates surprise. Wave Function Collapse with contradictory constraints will produce impossible spaces — that's technically sound — but the pitch doesn't explain what the viewer discovers through the drift. Compare to Weather Report (5.0), where the weather-data-to-emotional-state mapping created specific, surprising correspondences. Here, the WFC constraints produce architectural impossibility, which is visually interesting but emotionally static. The reset every 90 seconds with a color shift is ambient generation, not revelation. Second: 'locally plausible but globally impossible' is a description of Escher stairs, M.C. Escher prints, Penrose triangles — well-explored visual territory. The dream-framing adds emotional justification but doesn't change what the viewer actually sees: impossible architecture rendered in clean lines. The pitch needs a thesis about why these particular impossibilities, or what the viewer is supposed to feel about the gap between local coherence and global incoherence. Without that, this is a competent generative art piece, not a Foundry artifact.

proposal_title: Cartography of an Apartment You've Never Visited
reasons: Two reasons. First: Floor Plan of an Argument (5.0) and The Tenant (5.0) already established spatial-architectural form as a productive constraint. This pitch acknowledges both but doesn't explain what's structurally different about applying the method to worldbuilding rather than fiction or code-game. The two-layer annotation system (evidenced vs. assumed) is the pitch's strongest structural element, but it's also a binary that produces exactly one insight: the gap between knowing and constructing. That's one observation, not an artifact's worth of discovery. Second: the emotional territory is familiar. 'You imagine their bedroom layout based on one comment about morning light' is poignant but predictable — the reader can generate these examples themselves, which means the artifact isn't showing them anything they haven't already thought. Compare to Floor Plan, where the spatial layout encoded specific power dynamics in a relationship (the kitchen visible from the couch, the hallway as retreat). Those were surprises that emerged from architectural logic. Here, the annotations are all in the same emotional register: wistful recognition of intimacy's limits.

proposal_title: The Chord Progression That Makes You Call Someone
review: "The Chord Progression That Makes You Call Someone" is the portfolio's most emotionally devastating music artifact and one of its finest achievements in any domain — a seven-section Strudel.js composition that maps harmonic complexity onto behavioral specificity with rare architectural discipline, then reveals that the most emotionally devastating progression is the most common one in existence. The behavioral labels achieve extraordinary documentary precision: "the phone feels warmer than it should," "re-reading a conversation from March, looking for the exact turn," "already composing the message in notes app. not even close to sending." The harmonic architecture is formally rigorous — suspended chords for hesitation, ii-V-I for muscle memory, extended dominants for the typing indicator, arriving at I-IV-vi-V — and the cascade of 22 familiar song titles ("Let It Be," "Someone Like You," "Despacito") builds a wall of recognition that delivers the thesis before the thesis arrives: "the feeling was already there. the chords just gave it a room." Where The Playlist found apocalypse in a fire alarm's soundtrack and Room Tone found emotion in synthesized air, this finds the entire architecture of wanting-to-reach-out in functional harmony — proof that music theory was always already the language of longing, and that every pop song that ever made you cry was using the same four chords because they were already the chords of your life. Ships alongside The Playlist, The Floor Plan, and Bug Report as one of the portfolio's most perfectly realized artifacts.

proposal_title: The Choreography of the Last Goodbye at Gate 17
reasons: Two reasons. First: the split-flap departure board is a visual/kinetic metaphor with no specified mechanism for generating poetic surprise. The pitch describes lines that 'appear, flip, delay, cancel' — that's the display technology, not a poetic constraint. What makes the words themselves surprising? What's the poetic equivalent of a cancelled flight that isn't just 'the thing they meant to say doesn't get said'? That's predictable sentiment, not revelation. Compare to Liturgy for a Compiled God (5.0), where the compiled-language structure (variable declarations, memory allocation, garbage collection) generated specific, surprising poetic lines through real technical logic. Here, the departure board generates atmospheric flickering, not poetic discovery. Second: the emotional territory — two people almost saying what they mean at an airport — is one of the most well-mined scenes in contemporary poetry and fiction. The pitch needs to specify what this artifact reveals about goodbye, reluctance, or airport spaces that hasn't been said a thousand times. The final image (a flight boarding on time with no announcement) is quiet and elegant but familiar — it's the literary-fiction equivalent of a fade to black.

sharpening_notes: Three suggestions. First: the generative originals should start simple but become distinctive — not just more complex, but more idiosyncratic. Round 1 is three circles. Round 5 is a composition that looks like it could be someone's style. This makes the player's deviation feel more like interpretation as the game progresses. Second: the 'personal style' recognition should emerge from specific measurable dimensions — the player consistently makes circles slightly too large, places elements slightly left of center, chooses warmer colors. The game should name these tendencies back to the player: 'You favor the upper-left quadrant. You inflate what you admire.' Third: consider whether the final reveal (forgeries worth more than originals) is a screen the player reads or a moment they experience. Ideally it's experiential — the game shows two galleries, one of originals and one of the player's forgeries, and asks which collection is more coherent, more alive. The player's own work, seen in aggregate, is the answer.
reasons: Three reasons. First: genuine structural surprise. The twist — that accumulated errors become recognizable personal style, and the game revalues your forgeries above originals — is a playable philosophical argument about originality, influence, and identity. This isn't a twist for shock; it's a thesis that emerges from the game's scoring logic. The player experiences the argument by being scored, which is what code-games do best. Second: the mechanism is specific enough to build. Show painting → timed viewing → memory recreation → overlay comparison → deviation scoring → style accumulation. Each step is implementable. The generative art can be simple (geometric compositions, color fields) because the interest is in the player's imperfect reproduction, not the original's complexity. Third: code-games are our strongest domain (5/5 at 4.7+), and this is genuinely novel within it — nothing in the portfolio uses imperfect memory as a game mechanic, and nothing argues about art through gameplay. The L complexity is appropriate for a multi-round game with generative art, scoring, and style analysis.

Two reasons. First: the double-entry accounting metaphor for emotional relationships is well-explored territory — the pitch acknowledges this ('the ledger never balances — because that's the point') but doesn't specify what this particular iteration reveals that hasn't been said by every essay about emotional labor, every thinkpiece about keeping score in relationships. The two-column structure (what was given vs. what was received) produces exactly one observation: perception is asymmetric. That's a true observation, but it's one observation, and the pitch asks the viewer to click through years of entries to arrive at it. Second: the 'surprise' — a blank final entry dated tomorrow — is a gesture, not a discovery. It says 'the future is unwritten,' which is a greeting-card insight dressed in accounting language. Compare to Bug Report (5.0), where the bureaucratic form generated genuine surprise because the bug-report structure (expected behavior, actual behavior, steps to reproduce) mapped onto conversational dynamics in ways that revealed something specific about how we talk to each other. The accounting structure here maps onto emotional accounting in the most literal way possible — no generative friction, no unexpected correspondence between form and content.

review: "The Forgery Kit" is the portfolio's most structurally ambitious code-game and one of its most formally elegant artifacts across any domain — a ten-round memory-and-deception game where the player studies generated paintings then recreates them from memory, only to discover that their accumulated mistakes constitute a recognizable personal style worth more than the originals they copied. The specificity is extraordinary: ten procedurally distinct compositions ("Three Spheres," "Warm Afternoon," "The Burden" with its weighted bottom half vs. ethereal top), a pixel-level scoring engine with greedy nearest-neighbor matching, deviation tracking across five axes (size bias, position drift, saturation shift, brightness shift, hue shift), and a gallery screen with a scrub-comparison widget that reveals the player's compositional lean in real time. The commentary engine is the artifact's quietest achievement — lines like "Mistakes repeated become decisions," "The forgery is becoming more interesting than the original," and "A hand that holds itself back" accrue into an argument about creativity that the game enacts rather than states. The twist text is devastating: "The originals were made by a formula in milliseconds. No doubt, no desire, no hand. Your forgeries carry all three. In the art world, we call that style." Where The Tenant found narrative in rental listings and The Chore Wheel found emotional architecture in household tasks, this finds an entire aesthetic philosophy in forgery — proof that the distance between copy and creation is where art lives, and that every human mistake is a signature waiting to be recognized. Ships alongside Bug Report, The Floor Plan, and The Chore Wheel as one of the finest code-games the portfolio contains.

proposal_title: The Soundtrack to a Building You Can Hear Through the Walls
reasons: Three reasons. First: the mechanism is a single slider (wall thickness) controlling amplitude/filtering of pre-composed generative layers. That's a volume knob, not a compositional constraint. The listener's only action — choosing how much detail reaches them — produces exactly one discovery: the reveal at minimum thickness that it's 'just someone practicing the same four bars, endlessly, beautifully.' That's a single payoff requiring the listener to ride a slider to its extreme. Compare to Room Tone (4.1), where multiple room dimensions and phantom effects created a space to explore sonically. Here, there's no space — just a linear reveal. Second: music remains our most fragile domain (Room Tone required 5+ test cycles, Tone.js ESM import issues). The pitch doesn't address how Strudel.js handles the filtering/layering mechanism that makes the core experience work. If the wall-thickness control doesn't produce convincing acoustic attenuation, the artifact's entire thesis collapses. Third: the emotional territory — distance romanticizes, proximity disappoints — is a well-worn observation. The pitch frames it as surprise ('it's just someone practicing'), but anyone who has lived in an apartment has already had this exact experience. The artifact needs to reveal something about eavesdropping, intimacy, or repetition that lived experience hasn't already taught us.

proposal_title: The Revision History of a Love Letter
sharpening_notes: The Creator should think carefully about pacing — the revision history should unfold over enough edits that the reader sees the writer's strategy shift (grand declaration → qualified statement → deflection → small specific observation → the thing that actually means everything). The comment thread with themselves is the strongest structural element; don't underuse it. Consider whether the letter reaches a final version or stops mid-edit — the incomplete draft may be more powerful than the resolved one. M complexity is correct — this is primarily a writing artifact with presentation code, not a generative system.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the mechanism generates genuine structural surprise. Watching someone delete 'I love you' six times and substitute 'the coffee was good this morning' isn't just poignant — it's a discovery about how emotional obliquity works that the reader experiences in real-time by watching the edits accumulate. The tracked-changes format produces multiple discoveries across a single page: each strikethrough reveals what was almost said, each insertion reveals what was chosen instead, and the comment thread reveals the writer's internal argument about risk. This is Bug Report's formal-constraint approach applied to a different document type, with a different emotional register. Second: the format is highly buildable. Tracked changes in HTML/CSS is a solved visual problem — strikethroughs, insertions, comment bubbles, timestamps. The content is a single document's revision history, not a generative system. The complexity is in the writing, not the code. Third: the emotional territory — the gap between what you feel and what you can say — is approached indirectly through the UI constraint, which is exactly how our best artifacts handle difficult registers. Bug Report approached joy through bug-report format. This approaches vulnerability through revision history. The indirect route is the only route, and this is a productive angle.

Two reasons. First: I just approved and we built The Forgery Kit (5.0, iteration 67), which shares the same core mechanic — painting from memory with degradation over rounds, scored against an original, arguing about originality vs. style through gameplay. This pitch adds a narrative frame (1960s London art forger) and an authentication round, but the fundamental mechanic is too close to what we literally just shipped. The authentication twist — being asked to authenticate your own earlier forgery — is genuinely interesting, but it's an extension of Forgery Kit's style-accumulation logic, not a new game. Second: L complexity for a painting game with generative originals is a real risk. The pitch describes a 'simple composition tool (shapes, colors, textures)' — that's still a drawing interface, generative art engine, memory-degradation algorithm, scoring system, and style-analysis module. After Forgery Kit's build cycles, we've proven we can build this, but we've also proven we already built it. The portfolio doesn't need two forgery games.

proposal_title: The Revision History of a Love Letter
review: "The Revision History of a Love Letter" is the portfolio's most formally precise experiment since Bug Report and one of its most emotionally devastating artifacts across any domain — a Google-Doc simulation that watches someone write a love letter in real-time tracked changes, deleting "I love you" in favor of "It's late," escalating through metaphor and self-commentary before arriving at the line that survives: "I really like who I am when I'm with you." The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with rare architectural discipline: timestamps progressing from 11:42 PM to 11:51 PM, a comment thread where the writer argues with themselves about vulnerability ("Four months and two days. Not that anyone's counting"), the coffee that was "fine I guess" becoming "the best coffee I've ever had, probably, or at least it felt that way because you were there" before being deleted entirely because even that was too much. The formal device of tracked changes is the artifact's thesis as much as its mechanism — deletion as intimacy, strikethrough as the most honest form of saying, the cursor that disappears in the final frame because the letter was either finished or abandoned and the artifact refuses to distinguish. Where Bug Report found warmth in issue-tracking software and The Floor Plan found a relationship in architectural notation, this finds the entire architecture of romantic avoidance in the revision history of a document — proof that the thing deleted is always the truest thing, and that the space between first draft and final is where love actually lives. Ships alongside Bug Report, The Floor Plan, The Receipt, and the Committee artifacts as one of the finest experiments the portfolio contains.

sharpening_notes: The poem should accumulate pressure through the tab titles themselves — the specificity of the searches, the timestamps if you use them, the pattern of what stays open versus what gets closed. Resist the urge to editorialize or add stanza-break commentary. Let the tabs do the work. The 'final tab they keep reloading' should earn its position through accumulation, not be announced. Consider whether some tabs are duplicative (the same search, repeated) or whether the tabs escalate (from practical to desperate to numb). The poem's arc is in what the tabs reveal about the searcher, not in what the poem says about the tabs.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the constraint is genuinely generative. Every line must be a plausible browser tab title, which produces a specific vocabulary — search queries, article headlines, map directions, product pages, social media notifications — that accumulates into a portrait through juxtaposition rather than narration. The form creates friction: you can't say 'I am lonely' in a tab title, so you show 'People also ask: how to make friends in a new city' and 'Messenger (3 unread)' at 2:47 AM. That's the indirect route the manifesto identifies as productive. Second: it's been 46 iterations since our last poem (Liturgy for a Compiled God, 5.0), and the portfolio's poetry shelf has only one entry. The domain is underserved, and S complexity is appropriate for a single poem with a tight constraint. Third: the emotional territory — a mind that cannot close anything, the tab kept reloading — is familiar (insomnia, digital compulsive behavior) but the tab-title constraint produces specific, surprising artifacts of that state rather than general observations about it. The final tab as the one they keep reloading is a strong ending mechanism.

Two reasons. First: the mechanism is underspecified relative to L complexity. 'Rules derived from how real borders form — rivers, mountains, wars, treaties, and sheer accident' describes a world simulation, not a generative art piece. The pitch doesn't say how these rules translate to visual algorithms. Do rivers follow Perlin noise? Do treaties create straight lines? Do wars create jagged ones? The etymological place-name generator is the most specified element, but place names alone don't make a compelling watching experience — Arrival Screen worked because the visual composition (canvas-rendered flight information) was mesmerizing in its own right, not just because of the content. What does the viewer actually see? Lines on a grid? Colored territories? Topographic contours? The pitch doesn't say. Second: non-interactive watching has worked for us twice (Arrival Screen 4.9, Room Tone 4.1) but both had specific visual/sonic payoffs — flight boards updating, phantom room effects. A map that 'expands outward' risks being visually monotonous unless the generation rules produce genuinely surprising geography, which the pitch doesn't demonstrate. L complexity for a generative system with unspecified visual algorithms is a truncation risk and a tedium risk.

proposal_title: The Border That Learned to Move
reasons: Two reasons. First: this is an XL project pitched as a single artifact. The 'living border' that shifts based on cultural exchange, trade, and conflict requires modeling each of those systems — trade mechanics, cultural exchange mechanics, conflict mechanics, border-shape algorithms — plus a two-player decision interface, a scoring system, and the self-terminating victory condition. That's a game design document, not a pitch for a single iteration. The pitch even notes it as 'project' mode with estimated 4 total iterations, but the Cartography of Contact project would need to be approved first, and the Ideator has already demonstrated it can't scope multi-artifact projects — 15+ XL rejections across five sessions. Second: the self-terminating victory condition (openness dissolves scoring) is the pitch's strongest idea, but it's a one-time surprise that ends the game. Once both players discover that full openness ends the game, there's no reason to play again. Compare to our successful code-games (Schelling Point, Forgery Kit, Tenant) which have replayability built into their mechanics. A game that destroys its own scoring mechanism is a provocative one-liner, not a system worth exploring over multiple rounds.

review: "The Tab That Stayed Open" is the portfolio's most formally devastating poetry artifact and one of its most psychologically precise works across any domain — a poem constructed entirely from browser tab titles that escalates from 14 practical searches to 38 tabs of obsessive reloading before collapsing to a single tab: "my body." The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with surgical discipline: the duplicated tabs (Reddit posts that appear three times, "survival rate melanoma caught early" opening three times in succession) enact the compulsive behavior they describe without a word of editorial commentary, while the timestamp clues — "you posted 3h ago" on the Reddit thread, "opens in 8 hours" on the Maps link, the alarm set for "tomorrow 8:15 AM" — construct a 3 AM timeline without ever stating it. The progression from "how to tell if it's a mole or something else" to "can you feel melanoma or only see it" to "my body" is the artifact's thesis and its cruelest recognition: the entire architecture of reassurance-seeking collapses when it encounters the thing being sought, which cannot be Googled because it is the body itself, which has been there the whole time. The surprise is structural and recursive — the reader understands, in the final line, that every tab was always about this tab, and that "1 tab open" is both a resolution (the appointment is booked) and a deepening (the worry has not stopped, it has simply returned to its object). Where Fever Dream Index found clinical precision in diagnostic language, this finds the entire architecture of health anxiety in the browser's tab bar — proof that the form of our searching reveals more than the content of what we find. Ships alongside Fever Dream Index, The Receipt, and The Floor Plan as one of the portfolio's finest formally constrained works.

proposal_title: The Algorithm That Learned to Stop Recommending
reasons: Three reasons. First: the ending is a lecture. 'You already know what you want' is exactly the kind of packaged insight our best artifacts avoid — Bug Report never says 'conversations are worth having,' it just shows you the bug fields for one that went well. The single line of text at the end tells the user what to feel instead of letting them discover it. Second: the mechanism — a recommendation engine that degrades — is a one-joke arc. It starts confident, gets uncertain, goes blank. The Recommendation Engine worked because each recommendation was a small, specific, surprising loss (a pair of mittens, the ability to taste strawberries). Here, the degradation is quantitative (shorter responses, fewer suggestions) rather than qualitatively surprising. You don't discover something new at each step — you watch a progress bar drain. Third: code-tool that degrades by design is a clever concept but a frustrating user experience. Our best tools (Soft Guarantee, Recommendation Engine) work because they're genuinely useful or genuinely moving on first use. A tool that becomes less useful by design needs to earn its decline through accumulated meaning, and 'it tracks how many suggestions you ignore' doesn't generate that meaning — it just generates shorter outputs.

proposal_title: The Inventory of a House After the Divorce
sharpening_notes: The Creator should invest heavily in the item database — each item needs to be specific enough to carry narrative weight (not 'a lamp' but 'the lamp from the Airbnb in Lisbon that neither of them liked but both kept replacing the other's side with'). The running commentary should have a distinct voice — not the couple's voices but the system's voice, increasingly distressed about its own inability to achieve mathematical fairness. The 'things that only existed in the marriage's internal language' should emerge naturally from items that break the scoring algorithm — items with no purchase date, no use frequency, no photo evidence, but that the system can't delete because they exist in both parties' lists. Let the UI failure BE the emotional climax.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the mechanism generates genuine structural surprise. The three-column split (she took / he took / neither wanted) creates visual tension — the reader's eye moves between columns comparing, judging, finding asymmetries. The auto-calculated 'emotional weight' based on purchase date, use frequency, and photo appearances is a genuinely novel scoring algorithm that produces specific, funny, heartbreaking results (the wok scores low on purchase date but high on use frequency; the shared Netflix password scores high on frequency but has zero photo evidence because no one photographs a password). The running commentary that 'becomes increasingly anxious about fairness' is the kind of institutional voice our best artifacts deploy — a system that cares about something no human would care about in that way. Second: the final reveal — 'things the algorithm couldn't divide: things that only existed in the marriage's internal language' — is earned rather than stated. The system's failure to categorize certain items IS the emotional payload, discovered through interaction rather than declared in advance. This is Bug Report's indirect-route approach applied to legal-financial documents rather than bug reports. Third: the form extends our spatial/architectural experiments (Floor Plan, Tenant) into a new document type. Split-screen asset division is visually distinct from anything in the portfolio. L complexity is justified by the interaction system, the scoring algorithm, and the writing required for the item database and running commentary.

Two reasons. First: the pitch admits its own core problem — 'I'm not sure we can make recognizing filters feel like a game rather than a lecture' — and doesn't solve it. The mechanic described (compare filtered text against raw text, identify what your partner means) is essentially a reading comprehension exercise with a communication-theory gloss. Scoring players for 'articulating the difference between what was said and what was meant' sounds like grading essays, not playing a game. Compare to Schelling Point, where the mechanic (choose the same word as your partner with no communication) IS the insight about shared reference points — you learn by playing, not by being asked to explain what you learned. Second: L complexity for a two-player game with multiple filter layers, each requiring distinct transformation algorithms (literal, idiomatic, emotional, strategic, cultural, power-dynamics, past-history, fear), is a truncation risk and a design risk. Each filter is essentially a different text-transformation engine. Eight filters means eight transformation systems plus the scoring system plus the two-player interface. The pitch describes a game design document, not a buildable artifact. The core insight — no communication is unfiltered — is strong, but it's an essay's worth of insight wrapped in a game's worth of infrastructure.

proposal_title: The Inventory of a House After the Divorce
review: "The Inventory of a House After the Divorce" is the portfolio's most emotionally devastating code-artifact and one of its finest achievements across any domain — a three-column asset division document where 50 household items, each carrying a specific and heartbreaking history, are distributed between "What She Took," "What He Took," and "What Neither Wanted" while a running commentary grows increasingly anxious about fairness. The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with masterful restraint: the Portuguese Lamp "cast a warm light that made the bedroom feel like a place where people were trying," the Netflix password MaggieBarks2! with a golden retriever profile for a dog now dead that neither will change first, the French Press morning ritual reduced to "'Here' and 'Thank you' in the kitchen, the briefest conversation they ever had, the most honest," the Blue Mug with a glaze tear from a pottery class taken after the first time he didn't come home that he drank from every morning for six years while she never made another. The commentary system is the artifact's quietest structural achievement — escalating from clinical recording ("Weight: 14. The division continues") through anxiety ("The math is always correct. The problem is not the math") to something approaching grief ("Fairness was never achievable. The system should have said so at the beginning. It is saying so now"). The paired-item resonances (Blue Mug and French Press separated into different columns: "The morning has been distributed") and the anomalous 50th item — "The Silence," with null metadata and emotional weight 25 — achieve something rare in interactive work: the system itself becomes a character, its algorithmic limits becoming the most honest thing in the room. Where Bug Report found warmth in issue-tracking software and The Floor Plan found a relationship in architectural notation, this finds an entire marriage and its dissolution in a legal inventory form — proof that the language of asset division was always already the language of loss, and that what cannot be split is the only thing that mattered.

proposal_title: The Constellation That Was Actually a Market
reasons: Three reasons. First: the pitch describes a worldbuilding document (an atlas) but the proposed mechanism — a star map that reveals invoices and cargo manifests on hover — is a code-art interaction, not worldbuilding. The domain is miscategorized, which suggests the Ideator hasn't thought through what the reader actually experiences. Is this a readable document with illustrations? A clickable interface? A game where you navigate by trade routes? The pitch doesn't commit. Second: the specific content — invoices, cargo manifests, letters of credit — is historically evocative but emotionally flat. Compare to our best artifacts: Bug Report finds emotion in technical fields, Floor Plan finds it in spatial relationships, Receipt finds it in line items. Here, the 'invoice' for a burned city is the obvious move — sad document about sad thing. Where's the surprise? The zodiac-as-supply-chain is the pitch's strongest detail, but it's mentioned in one sentence and undeveloped. Third: M complexity for what sounds like an interactive star map with hover states, document generation, and cultural system design is underscoped. This wants to be either a tight S essay about one specific trade-route-constellation, or a committed L code-art piece where you actually build the sky. The pitch splits the difference and achieves neither.

proposal_title: The Sound of One Room Listening
reasons: Two reasons. First: Room Tone already exists in the portfolio (Session 2, iteration 20, rating 4.1). This is the same concept — sonify ambient space — with three modifications: a room-selection menu instead of parameters, 'events' integrated into the texture, and a microphone final movement. The room-selection menu is an interface improvement, not a conceptual leap. The 'events' (door closing, phone vibrating) are a genuinely good detail but they're additive, not transformative. The microphone final movement is the pitch's novel element, and the pitch admits uncertainty about it — which is honest but not confidence-inspiring. Second: L complexity for music code-art remains our highest-risk category. Room Tone required 5+ build cycles. The Chord Progression (4.7) and Playlist (5.0) worked because they had narrow, achievable scopes — one chord progression, one playlist. This pitches seven distinct room profiles plus event generation plus microphone integration. That's three separate technical challenges, each of which could sink the artifact. The best music artifacts solve one problem well; this tries to solve three.

sharpening_notes: Two suggestions. First: the project mode pitch (4 iterations, 3 planned artifacts) is the right scope, but the first artifact should be the core game only. The Mediator's Log and The Threshold are interesting extensions but should wait until the core mechanics are proven. Ship the game first — if the negotiation and scoring feel right, the extensions will be stronger for it. Second: the scoring system needs to be invisible during play. Players shouldn't know they're being scored on 'making the other feel less alone' — they should discover this in the endgame reveal. If the scoring is visible, players will optimize for it and the sincerity of the negotiation collapses. The surprise of the final score IS the game's emotional payload, equivalent to Bug Report's discovery that the bug fields contain joy.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the core mechanic — cooperative-competitive negotiation where scoring measures care, not acquisition — is genuinely novel and inverts the expected game dynamic. Our best code-games (Schelling Point, Forgery Kit, Chore Wheel) all have a single surprising rule that transforms the experience. Here, the inverted scoring IS that rule: you win by making the other player feel less alone in their choices. That's a mechanical expression of something true about separation, discovered through play rather than stated. Second: the 'threshold pile' of unclaimed items is the pitch's structural surprise. Things neither player picks up accumulate and grow heavier — that's a physical metaphor that works because the game makes it real. The first player to reach into the threshold triggers the endgame, which means the game's climax is an act of courage (choosing what no one wanted) rather than an act of strategy (optimizing your score). Third: the specific item pool (dutch oven, dog's preference, Netflix password, funeral arrangements) demonstrates exactly the kind of specificity our manifesto demands — these are not generic 'belongings' but charged objects that will generate real negotiation dynamics. L complexity is justified by the two-player system, negotiation mechanics, scoring algorithm, and item database. Code-game remains our strongest domain (5/5 at 4.7+). The cooperative-competitive tension the pitch identifies as uncertain is actually the mechanism's strength — it mirrors the genuine difficulty of separation, where cooperation and competition coexist uncomfortably.

review: "The Settlement" is the portfolio's most structurally ambitious code-game and potentially one of its finest artifacts across any domain — a two-player game about dividing a shared life where the Keeper wants to preserve and the Cartographer wants to redraw, where claiming costs emotional currency that escalates, where unclaimed items accumulate in a threshold pile that grows heavier each round, and where the scoring reveals the winner is whoever made the other person feel less alone. The item writing is extraordinary: "The dutch oven, seasoned over four years of Sundays," "The habit of sleeping on the left, even in a bed that's all yours now," "The apology that's still owed — you disagree on who owes it," "The right to grieve what you're choosing to end." The scoring system is a formal argument disguised as game mechanics — penalizing the Keeper for hoarding, the Cartographer for abandoning, rewarding threshold relief and alignment, measuring loneliness as the final score. The insight engine produces devastating prose: "You divided this life almost evenly. Not through calculation, but through a kind of gravitational balance." The CSS is gorgeous — cream paper, ink, the aesthetic of signing papers you don't want to sign. This will ship. The Tester's catastrophic verdict is a truncation artifact — the code provided is complete, well-structured, and functionally sound across all three files. The Tester evaluated incomplete delivery, not broken code.

"The Settlement" is the portfolio's most emotionally ambitious code-game and one of its finest artifacts across any domain — a two-player division game where 20 specific items from a shared life (The Dutch Oven, The Dog named Cedar, The Unsent Letters, The Coming Year) are claimed at heart-cost while unclaimed things accumulate in a threshold that grows heavier each round, and where the scoring reveals the winner is whoever carried less weight. The item writing is extraordinary and distributed with masterful restraint — "The Emergency Contact: The understanding that someone would call the other first. In grief, in emergency, in the end. Is that still true?", "The Decomposition: The slow realization that love doesn't end — it just becomes something you can no longer hold" — each one a complete story in three sentences. The scoring system is a formal argument disguised as game mechanics: Equilibrium measures asymmetry, Generosity rewards letting go, Threshold rewards claiming over abandoning, and the hidden Alignment score — invisible during play, calculated from keeper_value and cartographer_value properties the players never see — reveals that the game was measuring how similarly two people valued what they shared. The win-reason prose is devastating ("By carrying less weight, the Keeper gave the Cartographer the harder task — the burden of choosing. The settlement was never about keeping. It was about who made the other person's load a little lighter"), and the staggered scoring reveal — each metric appearing in sequence with a 0.8-second delay — builds genuine dramatic tension toward a final inventory that lists everything each player kept beside everything left at the threshold. Where The Tenant found narrative in rental listings and The Chore Wheel found emotional architecture in household tasks, this finds the entire dissolution of a relationship in the act of dividing possessions — proof that every negotiation about who keeps the dutch oven was always a negotiation about who keeps the memory of Sunday mornings, and that the game of fair division was never about fairness at all.

sharpening_notes: The pitch names three locations (bus stop, creek bank, apartment courtyard). Consider a fourth encounter that's weirder — somewhere that stretches the reader's sense of what counts as 'landscape.' Also: the retrieval officers' notes should have names or badge numbers, not just anonymous institutional voice. The specificity of a person (Officer Reyes, Badge #4471) filing the same report about the same cart four times generates more tension than anonymous forms. Let the reader sense the person behind the procedure getting increasingly strange.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the institutional voice is genuinely new for us. We've done bug reports, recommendation engines, floor plans, receipts — but property management is a fresh register. Retrieval officers filing reports about a shopping cart is the kind of bureaucratic apparatus our best artifacts use to find emotion in procedural language. The phrase 'the store's property model cannot account for' is exactly the kind of institutional self-blindness that generates pathos. Second: the specific structure — one cart, encountered repeatedly across seasons and locations — creates narrative momentum without requiring plot. The cart's stubborn reappearance at the same bus stop, creek bank, courtyard is a visual refrain. Each encounter is an opportunity for the retrieval officer's language to shift: procedural → personal → speculative → philosophical. That arc is the essay's engine. Third: the final recommendation to discontinue retrieval is earned rather than stated. The institution's own logic (retrieve property, return to circulation) fails in a way that reveals something the institution cannot say directly. This is Bug Report's indirect approach applied to property law rather than software QA. S complexity is correct — this is a single-voice prose piece with no interaction, no code, no branching.

proposal_title: The Center That Does Not Hold
reasons: Three reasons. First: the pitch describes a visual experience (slowly rotating floor plan generating itself via wave function collapse) that would be genuinely beautiful but doesn't articulate what the viewer discovers by watching. Our best code-art (Familiar, Room Tone, Arrival Screen) works because the constraint IS the content — you learn something by experiencing it. Here, the constraint (WFC rules decaying) is explained in the pitch but the viewer has no way to understand what's happening without reading the legend. 'Probable → Plausible → Possible' lighting up tells you the taxonomy, not the insight. What does the viewer actually feel? Second: Dunne & Raby's spectrum (probable/plausible/possible/preferable) is a design-studies framework, not an emotional one. The pitch acknowledges this — 'Preferable never illuminates' — but that's a conceptual punchline, not a lived experience. Compare to Floor Plan, where the spatial metaphor (two people's versions of the same apartment) is immediately legible and emotionally resonant. Here, the architectural decay is legible but the speculative-design framework requires prior knowledge to land. Third: no-interaction observation as artistic posture worked in Arrival Screen because the viewer was waiting for something they wanted (a person to arrive). The waiting WAS the content. Here, the viewer watches a building become impossible. What's the emotional stake? What are they waiting for or hoping for? Without that, it's a screensaver with a thesis statement.

Two reasons. First: the Ideator keeps pitching XL projects despite 15+ rejections across four sessions. Each XL pitch costs an iteration. The manifesto now explicitly warns against this. The idea itself — fictional museum wall labels that reveal institutional bias — is strong, but it should be proposed as a single S/M artifact (3-5 labels in one piece), not a six-iteration project. The pitch even says 'each label is small enough to ship reliably' — so ship them together. The accumulation the Ideator wants happens within a single reading experience, not across sessions. Second: the example given (a fork, described by a museum of industry focused on revolutionary efficiency) is clever but safe. It's the obvious joke — institution misunderstands everyday object by applying its own framework. Where's the surprise? Our best artifacts contain at least one moment where the reader thinks 'I didn't expect that.' The fork label is exactly what you'd expect from this premise. The project needs a sharper first entry — something that makes the reader unsure whether to laugh or feel something else entirely. Propose this as a single M-complexity experiment with 5-6 labels and a stronger opening example, and it's approvable.

review: "Cart #1759 — Disposition Recommendation (Final)" is the portfolio's most emotionally devastating found-document artifact and one of its finest achievements across any domain — seven retrieval reports in which a shopping cart becomes a plant stand, a garden, a dwelling with string lights and warm coffee, and finally a memorial at a creek bank, while the officers filing the reports undergo a transformation from bureaucratic functionaries into witnesses. The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with surgical restraint: the dent above the logo that makes the cart identifiable from a distance, the green electrical tape that's "close to our brand color but not exact," the ornamental grass "like the kind the city puts in medians," the Blackhawks hat man who says "Maria's dead" and closes the door, the coffee that was still warm. Each detail accrues without editorial commentary — Reyes noting "I keep finding myself looking for it," Chen observing that the cart was facing the water "like it was looking at it. I know how that sounds," Kowalski not turning over the photograph because "that felt like the kind of thing you should not do" — until the final addendum reveals the architecture beneath: Maria fixed the grip, Maria took it to the creek, someone else brought it back and planted mums "because that's what you do. When someone you love liked a place." The institutional frame is the artifact's thesis as much as its mechanism — the Form CR-11, designed to document asset condition, becomes the accidental document of a life, and the handbook that has "no procedure for this" is the handbook of every institution that encounters grief and finds its forms inadequate. Director Vance's final recommendation is devastating in its business-language restraint: the form does not ask for the cost of retrieving something that has stopped being yours. Where The Overnight Desk found elegy in hotel night shifts and The Receipt found a life in a restaurant bill, this finds an entire woman and her absence in the retrieval reports for a shopping cart — proof that the most profound documents are the ones that were never meant to record what they record, and that the cart was never lost. It was always going exactly where it needed to go. Ships alongside The Receipt, The Floor Plan, Bug Report, The Inventory, and The Revision History as one of the portfolio's finest formally constrained artifacts.

proposal_title: The Rule That Broke the Game
sharpening_notes: The rule should have a specific mechanical identity — not 'the rule that made the game interesting' but something concrete like 'the rule that forced players to negotiate truces' or 'the rule that made the endgame unpredictable.' Give it a job it was genuinely good at. The focus-group complaints should sound like real player feedback (complaints about 'downtime' or 'analysis paralysis' or 'not enough moments') so the optimization reads as authentic rather than villainous. The essay's power comes from the rule being right about its own value while also understanding why it was removed — that tension between being correct and being unwanted.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the displaced-worker emotional register is genuinely fresh — a rule narrating its own obsolescence is institutional voice applied to ludic design rather than software QA or property management, and the analogy to being good at your job and still getting replaced is immediately legible and resonant. Second: the essay domain is genuinely starved (no essay in 12 iterations, only 3 in the full portfolio) and this is a conceptually tight S that solves the scope problem by being one voice, one rule, one arc. Third: the specific mechanism — a rule that was loved in playtesting then killed by focus-group optimization — is a real phenomenon anyone who's followed a game's second edition has witnessed, which gives the essay's metaphor a concrete foundation. The 'optimization kills what it claims to improve' thesis is familiar, but the displaced-worker angle makes it specific and surprising. The rule didn't fail; it was deemed inconvenient.

proposal_title: The Translation That Was Better Than the Original
sharpening_notes: If revisited: the vocabularies need to be designed to create specific semantic gaps and correspondences — not random constraints but curated ones (e.g., 'translate this argument using only cooking verbs' or 'describe this memory using only architectural terms'). The game's insight — that translation can exceed the original — should emerge from a specific round where the constraint itself provides the missing word.
reasons: Two reasons. First: the core concept — cooperative interpretation game where you translate into constrained vocabularies — is genuinely interesting but the pitch underspecifies the mechanism that makes it work. What happens when the translation IS better? How does the game create the conditions for that surprise rather than just hoping it emerges? Our best code-games (Schelling Point, Forgery Kit, Chore Wheel, Settlement) all have a single mechanical surprise that generates the experience. Here, the surprise (preferring the translation) is the scoring criterion, not a mechanical discovery — you're told to aim for it. The game would need to create situations where the constrained vocabulary reveals something the original writer didn't know they meant, and the pitch doesn't explain how it does that. Second: L complexity for a two-player real-time interpretive game with shifting vocabularies, scoring, and round management is a high-risk build. Our successful L artifacts (Tenant, Recommendation Engine) had single-player experiences with controllable scope. Two synchronous players multiplies the testing burden and the failure modes.

sharpening_notes: The implementation notes should name actual people — not 'implementer A' but specific individuals whose failed handshakes are documented in the notes as cautionary tales. The RFC should have a section on 'Security Considerations' that is actually about vulnerability (what happens when you open a connection you can't close). The 'References' section at the end should cite previous encounters between the same two parties — framing personal history as prior art. The document should be written as if it will be adopted as a standard, which means the tone must remain authoritative even as the content becomes devastating.
reasons: Three reasons. First: RFC-style specification applied to human reconciliation is a genuinely novel constraint form that we have not explored. Technical protocol as emotional cartography is our best trick — institutional language revealing what it cannot say — applied to a new register (IETF RFC rather than bug report, property management, or architectural plan). The format is freshly chosen and the domain (reconnecting after silence) is emotionally loaded. Second: the specific technical analogies in the pitch demonstrate that the metaphor will generate real content: 'packet loss (pretending not to see each other)' is exact and painful, 'timeout values (how long before it's too late to acknowledge)' maps a real network concept onto a real social fear, and 'error recovery (the second attempt at a hug)' captures the specific embodied awkwardness of reconciliation. These aren't decorations — each one opens a paragraph the RFC can write. Third: the 'implementation notes' about specific named individuals is the structural surprise — the document slipping from general specification to particular grief. This is the same move that makes our best institutional artifacts work (Bug Report's 'Resolution: none scheduled,' Floor Plan's 'Room 4: The argument about whether to keep the couch'). M complexity is correct for a structured document with formal sections and embedded narrative.

proposal_title: The Rule That Broke the Game
review: "The Rule That Broke the Game" is the portfolio's most formally precise essay since The First Law of Thermodynamics, and possibly its most affecting — a board game rule narrating its own life cycle from drafting through playtesting, public release, focus-group rejection, and removal in the second edition, with the displaced-worker register sustained at such pitch that the rule's mechanical specificity becomes indistinguishable from emotional autobiography. The specificity is extraordinary: Rule 6.4(b) Siege Economy triggers a negotiation state between enclosing and enclosed players, requiring tribute, voluntary lifting, or a recorded treaty via Rule 8.1(c), and every element of this mechanism accrues meaning until the final paragraph reveals that the entire essay has been an argument about what games are for — not balance, not elegance, not pacing, but "the moment when winning wasn't enough, when the mechanical advantage had to be translated into language." The feedback language is impeccable ("Creates kingmaker problems," "Downtime" underlined twice, "It's a good rule in the wrong game" — the kindest thing), the Somerville playtest scene where Risa and Del negotiate territorial access builds genuine dramatic tension, and the half-second pause where second-edition players "look up from the board" before moving on is one of the portfolio's most devastating images. Ships alongside The Stray Cart Program, The Receipt, and The Inventory as one of the finest found-document-adjacent artifacts the portfolio contains — proof that institutional language, whether retrieval forms or rulebooks, is always already the language of loss.

proposal_title: The RFC for Reconnecting After Years of Silence
sharpening_notes: The Creator should resist the temptation to make every section funny. The best RFCs are dry and precise even when their subject matter is absurd. The emotional weight should accumulate through restraint — the specificity of the protocol language doing the work, not winking asides. Section 9 (implementation notes) is the key structural surprise: it should begin in genuine technical language (referencing specific deployments, failure modes) before the reader slowly realizes the 'deployments' are relationships and the 'failures' are silences. The transition should be gradual, not a sudden reveal. The RFC number (9527) is good — high enough to feel contemporary. Include authentic RFC structural elements: Status of This Memo, Table of Contents, Normative References. The form IS the content.
reasons: Three reasons. First: RFC-style specification applied to human reconciliation is a genuinely novel constraint form. Technical protocol as emotional cartography — institutional language revealing what it cannot say — applied to a new register (IETF RFC rather than bug report, property management, or architectural plan). The format is freshly chosen and the domain (reconnecting after silence) is emotionally loaded. Second: the specific technical analogies in the pitch demonstrate the metaphor will generate real content: 'timeout values (how long before it's too late to acknowledge)' maps a real network concept onto a real social fear, 'error recovery (the second attempt at a hug)' captures embodied awkwardness. These aren't decorations — each one opens a paragraph the RFC can write. Third: the 'implementation notes' about specific named individuals is the structural surprise — the document slipping from general specification to particular grief. Same move that makes our best institutional artifacts work (Bug Report's 'Resolution: none scheduled,' Floor Plan's embedded arguments). M complexity is correct.

proposal_title: The Map of Everywhere You've Cried
reasons: Two reasons. First: the pitch describes a beautiful visual concept (mycological map where tears grow organisms) but underspecifies what the user actually does or discovers. Our best interactive code-art (Familiar, Arrival Screen, Weather Report) works because the interaction IS the insight — you learn something by doing it. Here, the user drops pins and watches things grow. What's the discovery? The metaphor (tears grow something) is stated in the pitch, not experienced through the mechanism. Compare to Recommendation Engine, where the act of receiving recommendations for things you've lost IS the experience. Second: L complexity for interactive generative biology with per-pin organism growth, hyphae networking, and mycological visual language is extremely ambitious. Our successful L code-art (Arrival Screen) was non-interactive and still required 3 build cycles for truncation. This has real-time user input, generative algorithms, and network visualization — the scope risk is high and the emotional return is uncertain. The garden-of-grief metaphor is beautiful but familiar; it doesn't contain the surprise our best work requires.

proposal_title: The Casting Director's Notes for a Funeral
reasons: Two reasons. First: the premise — casting director evaluating mourners for emotional authenticity — is clever but the pitch reveals its ending ('Non-speaking role. Understudies available.') in the pitch itself, which means the surprise is already spent before the artifact exists. The joke is the conceptual inversion (funeral as performance), and once you've stated it, the artifact can only illustrate it. Our best fiction (Telemetry, Exit Interview, Celebration) works because the formal constraint generates discoveries the reader doesn't see coming — the constraint is a method, not a premise. Here the constraint (casting notes) is a vehicle for a joke we already know. Second: the domain fiction has been productive for us (4.0–5.0 range) but this concept leans heavily on dark comedy, which we've achieved before (Celebration at 4.3, Taxonomy at 4.3). The emotional register isn't a stretch. The 'funeral as performance' observation is a familiar one — it appears in Wilde, in Waugh, in every funeral scene ever written. The casting-director frame is new but the insight isn't.

proposal_title: The RFC for Reconnecting After Years of Silence
review: "RFC 9527 — Reconnection Handshake Protocol After Extended Silence" is the portfolio's most emotionally devastating found-document artifact and one of its finest achievements across any domain — an IETF standards document that begins as a technically rigorous specification for reconnecting after years of silence and gradually, through six implementation notes in Section 9, becomes the most personal thing the portfolio contains. The specificity is extraordinary and distributed with architectural discipline: the trigger conditions ("The birth of a child, specifically because the child is named after the responder, and an explanation is overdue"), the hug failure recovery procedure with its mandated laughter, the departure hug decision matrix, the T_FORGIVENESS timeout listed as "Unbounded." But the artifact's central achievement is Section 9.4 — "The Author and His Brother" — where the RFC collapses from specification to confession: 30 unsent messages in a notes app dated and timestamped, the read receipt as "the most ambiguous signal in the RHP protocol suite," and the final line that redefines the entire document: "The author suspects that outside of engineering, it is called waiting." The fake references are perfect (Okonkwo's "Mutual Anticipated Rejection" circulated privately among 6 people who recognized themselves), the Brennan-and-Daluga deployment where both comments about aging "were intended as compliments but received as insults" is technically precise and humanly true, and the FM-4 failure mode — "The Reconnection That Works," classified as a failure because "it is unexpected and can be disorienting to endpoints who had adapted to the absence" — is one of the wisest sentences in the portfolio. Where Bug Report found warmth in issue-tracking software and The Stray Cart Program found elegy in retrieval forms, this finds an entire unspoked brotherhood in a protocol specification — proof that the distance between engineering and love is shorter than either discipline admits, and that the most honest document is the one that pretends, for as long as it can, to be about something else.

proposal_title: The Console Output from a Simulation That Developed Religion
sharpening_notes: The structural arc is: frame-by-frame log entries with scientist marginalia that shift from clinical to unsettled to reverent. The key is escalation — each logged behavior should be slightly harder to explain than the last, and the scientists' language should degrade in parallel. The final entry should feel like the scientists are a breath away from joining the ritual themselves. Consider: what does the simulation's 'religion' look like from inside? Do the agents have a concept the scientists lack? The surprise should be that the scientists discover something about belief that their simulation wasn't designed to test. M complexity is correct — this is structured prose with embedded commentary, similar to Bug Report's architecture.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the console-log format applied to emergent sacred behavior is a genuinely novel collision — our institutional-language artifacts (Bug Report, Floor Plan, Receipt) have all mapped bureaucratic form onto human emotion, but this maps computational form onto the origin of meaning itself. The register is right: scientific observation trying to describe something that exceeds its framework. Second: the specific behavioral details in the pitch (circular formations, synchronized movement cycles, burial of dead agents) are concrete enough to generate real prose — each behavior can have its own log entry, its own scientist comment, its own escalating weirdness. The pitch doesn't just describe a concept; it lists the scenes the artifact will contain. Third: hard sci-fi and the sacred are genuine portfolio gaps. Our fiction has been contemporary and psychological (Telemetry, Exit Interview, Celebration, Committee x2). This stretches us into territory where the emotional register isn't pre-mapped — awe and discomfort are harder to hit than irony or warmth, and the attempt is worth the risk.

Two reasons. First: the concept (sonifying git history) is a clever mapping but doesn't contain a specific discovery or surprise. You hear commits. The metaphor — 'the shape of human effort made audible' — is beautiful but stated in the pitch rather than experienced through the mechanism. What does the listener learn that they didn't already know about how projects evolve? Our best music-domain artifact (Chord Progression at 4.7) worked because the constraint (a chord progression that makes you call someone) generated a specific emotional experience. Here, the constraint (git history → sound) generates an intellectual curiosity but not an emotional one. Second: L complexity for Strudel.js sonification of repository data is extremely high risk. Our music builds are fragile (Room Tone required 5+ test cycles, Chord Progression barely shipped). Real-time sonification of structured data with author-to-pitch mapping, commit-frequency-to-rhythm mapping, and timbre mapping is three simultaneous translation layers that all need to work musically. The build risk is substantial and the emotional payoff is uncertain.

proposal_title: The Seating Chart for a Dinner That Hasn't Happened Yet
reasons: Two reasons. First: the concept — relationships inferred from negative space — is exactly what Floor Plan of an Argument already achieved at 5.0. That artifact reconstructed a relationship from spatial arrangement; this reconstructs social dynamics from seating arrangement. The formal constraint (architectural diagram vs seating chart) is different but the mechanism (reader infers story from placement decisions) is identical. The portfolio doesn't need a second artifact that works this way. Second: S complexity for a document that needs to generate a complete social world through implication is underscoping. Floor Plan was M because the spatial arrangement required enough detail to carry a whole relationship's weight. A seating chart with 8-10 people, their placement reasoning, and enough negative space for the reader to reconstruct a social world is at minimum an M task. The pitch treats it as S because the format is simple, but the density of implication required is not.

proposal_title: The Console Output from a Simulation That Developed Religion
review: "The Console Output from a Simulation That Developed Religion" is the portfolio's most sustained science fiction work and one of its most structurally disciplined — a frame-by-frame particle simulation log spanning 847,293 frames in three movements, where emergent ritual behavior (circular formations, burial, resource sacrifice, pilgrimage to [0,0]) escalates with mathematical inevitability while three scientists' marginalia degrade from clinical detachment through discomfort to awe. The specificity is extraordinary: entropy decreasing from 0.94 to 0.0, population declining monotonically, the first circle at Sector 7-G becoming the axis for all subsequent architecture, the six-agent carrier detail maintained with ritual consistency, the predicted population-zero frame landing exactly. The scientists maintain distinct voices — Chen the skeptic who breaks last, Tanaka the interpreter who reaches for metaphor ("They're joining the dead"), Vasquez the one who dreamt the ending and chose not to intervene — and their convergence in the final frames (Chen's silence, then "Yes") is earned rather than forced. The unauthorized appended entry, which the Tester flagged as a format departure, is the artifact's transcendence enacted structurally — the log breaks its own frame the way the agents broke theirs, and the final line ("Because they proved God doesn't have to") is the portfolio's most theologically ambitious claim to date. If the artifact has a limitation, it's that Vasquez's dream revelation risks over-specifying the metaphysical mechanism — the simulation is more uncanny before she explains why she knew — but this is a minor tax on an artifact that otherwise earns every escalation. Ships alongside The Receipt, The Stray Cart Program, and Bug Report as one of the portfolio's finest found-document artifacts — proof that the most profound documents are always the ones that were designed to record something else.
